subject: Help!! path analysis with observed variables of diverse types

messages.author: 70c506259cfb76e0
messages.subject: Help!! path analysis with observed variables of diverse types
parts:
Dear all,

I'm a nature science student, very new to SEM and lavaan, and I really need your help to evaluate the soundness of my methodology. In my study, I use path analysis to study carnivore-farmers conflicts in Eastern Honduras. My goal is to integrate the path analysis into a Causal Loop Diagram explaining socioeconomic implications in the shaping of stakeholders perceptions towards carnivores. 

The sample size is rather small: 104 observations. In my model, I include variables of different type, and with different levels, and this is the main challenge.

Exogenous Variables:

Residency time: continuous
Education level: ordinal, 4 levels: 1,2,3,4
Age: continuous
Ethnicity: binary (indigenous, non-indigenous)

Endogenous Variables:

a) Moderators
Adaptive Husbandry: binary (yes, no)
Acknowledgement Benefits: ordinal, 3 levels: -1,0,1
Engagement in Conservation: binary (yes,no)
Awareness Ecological Value: binary (yes no
b) Outcome variables
Tolerance: binary (yes,no)
Readiness to Denounce Poaching: binary (yes,no)
Acceptability Lethal Control: ordinal/likert, 5 levels: 1,2,3,4,5

I chose to treat the ordinal variables as numeric, because of the small sample size, using therefore Maximum Likelihood as estimator. I then studied the indirect effects to test the validity of the causal path. I scaled continuous variables to tackle the issue of extreme differences in variances, and used "fiml" to deal with NAs. 

here is the code in lavaan:

df_tolerance$residency_scaled <- scale(df_tolerance$residency)
df_tolerance$economic_loss_scaled <- scale(df_tolerance$economic_loss)
df_tolerance$age_scaled <- scale(df_tolerance$age)
df_tolerance$residency_clean_scaled <- scale(df_tolerance$residency_clean)

model_joint <- 'adaptive_husbandry ~ a1*residency_scaled + a2*ethnicity + a3*age_scaled + a4*education_level
                engagement_in_conservation ~ b2*acknowledgement_benefits
                awareness ~ acknowledgement_benefits
                acknowledgement_benefits ~ residency_scaled + education_level
                tolerance ~ b1*adaptive_husbandry + b4*awareness
                readiness_to_denounce ~ b3*engagement_in_conservation + age_scaled
                acceptability_lethal_control ~ acknowledgement_benefits + engagement_in_conservation
               

#indirect effects
IE_residency_tolerance := a1*b1
IE_ethnicity_tolerance := a2*b1
IE_age_tolerance := a3*b1
IE_residency_denounce := a1 * b2 * b3
IE_acknowledgement_denounce := b2 * b3
IE_acknowledgement_tolerance := b2* b4
IE_residency_tolerance2 := a1*b2*b4
IE_residency_lethal := a1*b2
IE_education_tolerance := a4*b1
IE_education_tolerance2 := a4*b2*b4
IE_education_lethal := a4*b2
'


fit_joint <- sem(model_joint, data = df_tolerance, missing="fiml")
summary(fit_joint, standardized=TRUE, fit.measures=TRUE, rsquare=TRUE)


The fit of the model is good, the regressions make sense and I hope I handled the data well. Although, small r² value are not entirely satisfying, but I hope the reason is that the sample is just very small.

messages.author: 0325c6a976085eab
messages.subject: Re: Help!! path analysis with observed variables of diverse types
parts:
First, that's a heck of a complex model for a pretty small sample size. 

Your specific questions:
1) (Considering the sample size) Do I need to use DWSL instead of ML? Even if I have a categorical ordinal variable as exogenous? In that case, do I have to set as "ordered" binary variables too?
No, I don't think your sample is large enough. I would be surprised it it converged / was identified (although there's no harm in trying). It took 40 iterations to converge, which is a lot.
2) Is there any other thing I have to think about while validating my model that I'm missing?
Not that are obvious to me.
3) Do You have any suggestions?

Your sample is too small to draw much in the way of conclusions. You have little power to reject the model if it is wrong (and a lot of parameters with large standard errors).

Your chi-square is not significant, but that's not a huge surprise at this sample size. Your null model is not awful, hence your TLI is not particularly high. The confidence intervals on your RMSEA are pretty wide.

The path diagram is not hugely clear to me (it's also very small, I can't read it). I try to make the diagram 'flow' from left to right - it looks like you have four exgoenous variables. Start with those four on the left, then these all have arrows pointing to the next two variables, etc.

Hope that helps (and wasn't too harsh),

Jeremy

messages.subject: Re: Help!! path analysis with observed variables of diverse types
parts:
It is a triangular system (the arrows flow in a specific direction, so you can write it up with demographics on top, and acceptability on the bottom, and the matrix of the coefficients to be estimated will be lower triangular). I'd say it should be estimated as an econometric simultaneous equations model (series of regressions), and not bother with formulating it as a latent variable model (which is what lavaan really expects). My understanding is that lavaan recognizes demographics as exogenous variables here, but since you asked for FIML, it still tries too hard to fit the model that is too reliant on multivariate normality. The reference I was able to find is https://bookdown.org/ccolonescu/RPoE4/simultaneous-equations-models.html (except of course rm(list=ls()) for which the author's computer should be burned, per Jenny Bryan's guidance).

No, I don't think your sample is large enough. I would be surprised it it converged / was identified (although there's no harm in trying). It took 40 iterations to converge, which is a lot.

2) Is there any other thing I have to think about while validating my model that I'm missing?

Not that are obvious to me.

3) Do You have any suggestions?

Your sample is too small to draw much in the way of conclusions. You have little power to reject the model if it is wrong (and a lot of parameters with large standard errors).

Your chi-square is not significant, but that's not a huge surprise at this sample size. Your null model is not awful, hence your TLI is not particularly high. The confidence intervals on your RMSEA are pretty wide.

The path diagram is not hugely clear to me (it's also very small, I can't read it). I try to make the diagram 'flow' from left to right - it looks like you have four exgoenous variables. Start with those four on the left, then these all have arrows pointing to the next two variables, etc.

Hope that helps (and wasn't too harsh),

Jeremy

Dear all,

I'm a nature science student, very new to SEM and lavaan, and I really need your help to evaluate the soundness of my methodology. In my study, I use path analysis to study carnivore-farmers conflicts in Eastern Honduras. My goal is to integrate the path analysis into a Causal Loop Diagram explaining socioeconomic implications in the shaping of stakeholders perceptions towards carnivores. 

The sample size is rather small: 104 observations. In my model, I include variables of different type, and with different levels, and this is the main challenge.

Exogenous Variables:

Residency time: continuous
Education level: ordinal, 4 levels: 1,2,3,4
Age: continuous
Ethnicity: binary (indigenous, non-indigenous)

Endogenous Variables:

a) Moderators
Adaptive Husbandry: binary (yes, no)
Acknowledgement Benefits: ordinal, 3 levels: -1,0,1
Engagement in Conservation: binary (yes,no)
Awareness Ecological Value: binary (yes no
b) Outcome variables
Tolerance: binary (yes,no)
Readiness to Denounce Poaching: binary (yes,no)
Acceptability Lethal Control: ordinal/likert, 5 levels: 1,2,3,4,5

I chose to treat the ordinal variables as numeric, because of the small sample size, using therefore Maximum Likelihood as estimator. I then studied the indirect effects to test the validity of the causal path. I scaled continuous variables to tackle the issue of extreme differences in variances, and used "fiml" to deal with NAs. 

here is the code in lavaan:

df_tolerance$residency_scaled <- scale(df_tolerance$residency)
df_tolerance$economic_loss_scaled <- scale(df_tolerance$economic_loss)
df_tolerance$age_scaled <- scale(df_tolerance$age)
df_tolerance$residency_clean_scaled <- scale(df_tolerance$residency_clean)

model_joint <- 'adaptive_husbandry ~ a1*residency_scaled + a2*ethnicity + a3*age_scaled + a4*education_level
                engagement_in_conservation ~ b2*acknowledgement_benefits
                awareness ~ acknowledgement_benefits
                acknowledgement_benefits ~ residency_scaled + education_level
                tolerance ~ b1*adaptive_husbandry + b4*awareness
                readiness_to_denounce ~ b3*engagement_in_conservation + age_scaled
                acceptability_lethal_control ~ acknowledgement_benefits + engagement_in_conservation
               

#indirect effects
IE_residency_tolerance := a1*b1
IE_ethnicity_tolerance := a2*b1
IE_age_tolerance := a3*b1
IE_residency_denounce := a1 * b2 * b3
IE_acknowledgement_denounce := b2 * b3
IE_acknowledgement_tolerance := b2* b4
IE_residency_tolerance2 := a1*b2*b4
IE_residency_lethal := a1*b2
IE_education_tolerance := a4*b1
IE_education_tolerance2 := a4*b2*b4
IE_education_lethal := a4*b2
'


fit_joint <- sem(model_joint, data = df_tolerance, missing="fiml")
summary(fit_joint, standardized=TRUE, fit.measures=TRUE, rsquare=TRUE)


The fit of the model is good, the regressions make sense and I hope I handled the data well. Although, small r² value are not entirely satisfying, but I hope the reason is that the sample is just very small.
